solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: In fiction, Fez is represented as great for models?

indicators.note: FEZ IS is represented in a new form, so its letters are rearranged
the scrambled letters go in the word for fiction

parts.note: a lie is a fiction
FEZ IS rearranged, placed inside LI…E

explanation.surface: A writer dresses a character in a fez, perhaps something grand enough to pose for artists.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a sly one: models built life-size are as great as the real thing, and the question mark owns up to the stretch.
explanation.definitionFit: A life-size model is as great, in scale, as its original, the fullest size a model can be.

clue.text: Group of composers — 9?

parts.note: the dash is read as a minus sign, spoken as 'less'
9 in Roman numerals

explanation.walkthrough: The dash looks like punctuation, and 9 looks like a cross-reference to another clue; in fact the dash is a minus sign and 9 is a Roman numeral. Les Six were six French composers of the 1920s, including Poulenc and Milhaud.
explanation.definitionFit: Les Six was the name given to a group of six French composers, among them Poulenc, Milhaud and Honegger.

clue.text: Films need high points?

indicators.note: high as in intoxicated, so the letters are all over the place

parts.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters

explanation.surface: A remark that films need big moments, dramatic peaks to keep an audience watching.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High points' reads as one phrase meaning climaxes; split it, and 'high' scrambles while 'points' stands alone. Point is a fielding position in cricket, so players stationed at point are fieldsmen.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket, point is a fielding position, so the players placed at point are, by example, fieldsmen.

clue.text: Comfort one draws from dictator

indicators.note: a dictator here is one who dictates, speaking words out for others to write down, so what follows is heard

parts.note: a sucker is one who draws liquid in

explanation.surface: Someone finds consolation in a tyrant, an unlikely source of kindness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dictator' looks like a tyrant but means one who dictates, speaking words aloud to a secretary.
explanation.definitionFit: Succour is help or comfort given in a time of need.

clue.text: These letters get edited in the production of gazettes

indicators.note: to edit something out is to cut it
the remaining letters are worked up into something new

parts.note: the starting word
G, E and T are cut out of GAZETTES, leaving AZTES

explanation.surface: An editor's note that certain letters get changed when newspapers are put together.
explanation.walkthrough: The G, E and T of 'get' are not together in GAZETTES; each is taken out separately, and the five letters left are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Zeta is the sixth letter of the Greek alphabet, so zetas are letters.

clue.text: Big bust controlled by ex-PM turned villain

indicators.note: the bust size is held in the hands of the ex-PM, so it sits inside
the ex-PM's nickname is turned round

parts.note: BoJo, the nickname of Boris Johnson
DD, a large bra cup size

explanation.surface: A former prime minister, involved in a big police raid, turns to crime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Big bust' looks like a police raid, but it is a bra size. Oddjob is the henchman with the steel-rimmed bowler hat in the Bond film Goldfinger.
explanation.definitionFit: Oddjob is Goldfinger's murderous henchman in the James Bond story, a classic screen villain.

clue.text: Help picking up D:Ream's notes audibly diminishing

parts.note: the letters of D:REAM that are musical notes: D, E, A

indicators.note: the word for diminishing is to be heard, not spelt

parts.note: to fade is to diminish

explanation.surface: A fan tries to catch the band D:Ream's music as it grows quieter.
explanation.walkthrough: D:Ream were a 1990s pop band whose 'Things Can Only Get Better' was a Labour anthem. 'Picking up' sounds like buying, but here it means hearing.
explanation.definitionFit: A deaf aid, an old name for a hearing aid, is a help to picking up sound.

clue.text: Spliff being shared with others

definitions.meaning: a spliff is a cannabis cigarette
held in common, like an account two people own together

explanation.surface: A cannabis cigarette is passed round a group.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is one scene, the joint being passed round, so the two meanings are hard to prise apart.
explanation.definitionFit: A joint is a cannabis cigarette, and joint means held or shared in common with others.

clue.text: Just lock pier

parts.note: but = just, as in 'but a child'
a tress is a lock of hair

explanation.walkthrough: Each word misleads: 'Just' looks like fair, 'lock' like a fastening, and 'pier' like a jetty rather than a supporting column.
explanation.definitionFit: A pier is a solid masonry support, and a buttress is such a support built against a wall.

clue.text: Writer left to probe case of sycamore tree

indicators.note: left goes probing into the outer letters

parts.note: the writer of the clue, speaking of himself

indicators.note: the case of a word is its outside letters

parts.note: the outer letters of SYCAMORE
left, as in quit a job

explanation.surface: An author walks off to examine the bark of a sycamore.
explanation.walkthrough: The sycamore is a decoy tree; the real one is the definition at the end. 'Writer' for ME is the setter referring to himself.
explanation.definitionFit: Mesquite is a thorny tree of the south-western United States and Mexico.

clue.text: For training perhaps, I see small children time and time again?

definitions.text: For training perhaps, I see small children time and time again?

indicators.note: training puts the letters through a regime that reshapes them

parts.note: anagram fodder
CH = children, the abbreviation
T = time, twice

explanation.surface: A professional explains they see young children again and again, for training.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the recipe and the definition: a speech therapist might say exactly this about their young patients.
explanation.definitionFit: A speech therapist sees small children repeatedly to train their speech, as the whole clue describes.

clue.text: Popular party or parties finally occupying the House

parts.note: in = fashionable, popular
a do is a party
used as it stands

indicators.note: only the final letter of parties is taken

parts.note: last letter of PARTIES

explanation.surface: A political party gains seats in the House of Commons.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The House' looks like Parliament, which fits the party politics; here it is any house, and being inside it is being indoors.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to occupy a house is to be inside it rather than out of doors; the capital H borrows the look of Parliament.

clue.text: Part of town square out of bounds — it's here, too

indicators.note: a word's bounds are its first and last letters, so these go
the same stripping applies to what follows

parts.note: SQUARE losing its first and last letters
IT'S losing its first and last letters
HERE losing its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A notice that a town square is off limits, and so is the spot where you stand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Too' tells you to treat 'it's' and 'here' exactly as you treated 'square'.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: towns divide into districts with their own character, and this word names one, as in the Latin Quarter of Paris.

clue.text: Italian lovers doing what lovers do: one delayed necking again

indicators.note: the I (one) is moved later in the phrase
the phrase swallows the next word, as when necking a drink

parts.words: doing what lovers do: one delayed
parts.note: AT IT (doing what lovers do), with the I moved to the end
more = again, as in 'once more'

explanation.surface: A couple in Italy kiss, and one of them lingers for another round of kissing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Necking' is kissing in the surface, but here it means swallowing, as you neck a pint. 'At it' is a coy British phrase for having sex.
explanation.definitionFit: Amoretti are cupids, the little winged love gods of Italian art; the word is Italian for little loves.

clue.text: Horse taking place of head of maths in private Oxford/Cambridge study?

indicators.note: the horse replaces the letter named

parts.note: a Tommy is a British private soldier
first letter of MATHS, the M removed
a pony is a small horse, put where the M was

explanation.surface: A student swaps maths for riding lessons in private study at Oxbridge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oxford/Cambridge study' suggests a university; it means the study of names like Oxford and Cambridge. Either M of TOMMY could go; the first gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Toponymy is the study of place names, and Oxford and Cambridge are place names.

clue.text: Very rich man is taking a fall

definitions.meaning: the name tradition gives the rich man in the Gospel parable of Lazarus
falls headlong, or goes down on purpose as a footballer does to win a foul

explanation.surface: A wealthy man takes a tumble, perhaps on the stock market.
explanation.walkthrough: Dives is the traditional name for the rich man in Jesus's parable of the rich man and Lazarus.
explanation.definitionFit: Dives is the name tradition gives the rich man in the Gospel parable; dives also means plunges or takes a fall.

clue.text: Marble entrance opened by five contracted stars

indicators.note: shortened, losing its last letter
the entrance has the other pieces at its front

parts.note: V = 5 in Roman numerals
ARIES, the constellation, shortened
a gate is an entrance

explanation.surface: A grand marble doorway, with five famous names engraved as you go in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Marble' is a verb here: to streak with colour, like marble. Stars can mean a constellation, here Aries.
explanation.definitionFit: To marble something is to streak it with irregular colours, which is to variegate it.

clue.text: Bonkers shot upset spinner

parts.note: a crack is a shot, an attempt

indicators.note: in a down clue, upset turns the word upside down

parts.note: a top spins

explanation.surface: A wild delivery unsettles the spin bowler in a cricket match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spinner' looks like a spin bowler in cricket; here it is the child's toy.
explanation.definitionFit: Crackpot, as an adjective, means eccentric or crazy, just as bonkers does.

clue.text: Narrow passageway runs from rear of waste-processing unit

indicators.note: the pieces are read from the back end forwards

parts.note: a lane is a narrow way
R = runs, in cricket scoring

explanation.surface: A narrow alley leads out from behind a sewage works.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface places a sewage plant; the waste-processing unit is the kidney, and 'of' makes the definition an adjective to match RENAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Renal means relating to the kidneys, the body's unit for filtering waste.

clue.text: Leaves to switch off TV programmes about cycling

indicators.note: turned about, so the letters run backwards
the letters go round in a loop, the front letter moving to the back

parts.note: to cut the power is to switch off
tele = television

explanation.surface: An instruction to turn off television shows about bike racing.
explanation.walkthrough: The reversal comes first, then cycling sends the front E round to the back. 'Cycling' pretends to be the subject of the TV programmes.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the leaves are the part of this salad plant that is eaten, so a head of it is a bunch of leaves.

clue.text: Encourage to release article backing chief of police force

indicators.note: the article is let go from the word
the shortened word comes behind, supporting the letter before it
only the head letter of police is used

parts.note: first letter of POLICE
to reassure is to encourage
A, the indefinite article, released from REASSURE

explanation.surface: A call to boost the police chief's morale by releasing a newspaper piece in his support.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Article' looks like a newspaper story, but it is the grammatical article A. 'Backing' puts RESSURE after P.
explanation.definitionFit: Pressure is force applied, physically or by persuasion.

clue.text: Was a parody spoilt with name dropping?

definitions.note: SPOOFED is a verb, 'parodied'; the clue stretches this to 'was a parody of'

indicators.note: the letter for name is dropped out

parts.note: spoon-fed = pampered, spoilt
N = name, dropped from SPOONFED

explanation.surface: A question whether a satire was ruined by a lot of name-dropping.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Name dropping' looks like the social habit; here it means the abbreviation N falls out.
explanation.definitionFit: To spoof something is to parody it, so what spoofed a work was a parody of it.

clue.text: Energy-saving routine plugged by Steve Jobs after vacating Apple

indicators.note: the routine keeps the energy safe inside
a plug is pushed into the middle

parts.note: a rut is a dull routine
E = energy, in physics

indicators.note: the names are emptied, leaving only their outer letters

parts.note: the outer letters of STEVE JOBS

explanation.surface: Steve Jobs, founder of Apple, pushes an energy-saving habit before leaving the company.
explanation.walkthrough: The Apple of the surface is the computer company; the definition is the fruit. The energy goes into the routine first, and the plug goes in after that.
explanation.definitionFit: A russet is a variety of apple with rough, brownish skin.

clue.text: Porridge server going outside to wipe floor with piece of toast

indicators.note: the porridge server's word goes around the other

parts.note: porridge is British slang for a prison sentence, served by a con (convict)
to wipe the floor with someone is to rout them

explanation.surface: A breakfast cook steps outside to clean the floor, toast in hand.
explanation.walkthrough: Porridge is British slang for time in prison, so the one serving it is a convict, CON.
explanation.definitionFit: A crouton is a small cube of fried or toasted bread, a piece of toast.

clue.text: Subject promoting work associated with faculty

indicators.note: the letters for work are moved up to the front

parts.note: OP = opus, a work, promoted to the front
TOPIC, a subject, with its OP taken out to be promoted

explanation.surface: A subject that advances research carried out within a university department.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Faculty' suggests a university department; here it is a faculty of the body, the sense of sight. The subject becomes the answer just by moving two of its letters up.
explanation.definitionFit: Optic means relating to the eye or sight, one of the body's faculties.

clue.text: Are changes accepted by you, no longer a social critic?

indicators.note: ARE changes into a new order
taken inside the archaic you

parts.note: thou, the archaic form of you
ARE rearranged, set inside THO…U

explanation.surface: A question to someone whether they have stopped being a critic of society once changes are accepted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No longer' reads as ceasing to be a critic, but it marks THOU as a word no longer used. Henry David Thoreau wrote Walden and 'Civil Disobedience'.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry David Thoreau, author of 'Civil Disobedience', was a sharp critic of society and government.

clue.text: Theatre doesn't have to worry, beginning to entertain a crowd?

indicators.note: the letters for worry are missing from theatre
only the first letter of entertain

parts.note: the starting word
first letter of ENTERTAIN, added at the end
EAT = worry, as in 'what's eating you?', removed, leaving THR…E

explanation.surface: A theatre is untroubled, starting to put on shows for a big audience.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition comes from the saying 'two's company, three's a crowd'; the question mark flags it.
explanation.definitionFit: The saying 'two's company, three's a crowd' makes three, by that reckoning, a crowd.

clue.text: Offended Lord Chancellor declines novel

parts.note: put out = offended
Sir Thomas More, Henry VIII's Lord Chancellor
to flag is to tire or decline

explanation.surface: A peer, insulted, turns down a book.
explanation.walkthrough: Put Out More Flags is Evelyn Waugh's 1942 novel. The Lord Chancellor is the head of the English judiciary, and Thomas More is its most famous holder.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: this 1942 Evelyn Waugh book, a comedy of the early war years, is a novel.

clue.text: Visitor coming from far away on flash travel pass?

indicators.note: in an across clue, the visitor sits on the end of the flash

parts.note: in a tick, in a flash
ET, the extra-terrestrial of the film

explanation.surface: A traveller arrives from a distant land and flashes a pass.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits the definition is loose: a ticket is a pass for a journey, not a pass that travels.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, loosely applied: this is the pass that lets you make a journey, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Drug contained in pop had a striking effect on down-and-out

indicators.note: the drug sits inside the word for pop

parts.note: pop = father
E = ecstasy
beat = struck repeatedly

explanation.surface: A drug slipped into a fizzy drink hit a homeless man hard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pop' looks like a fizzy drink but means father.
explanation.definitionFit: A deadbeat is an idle, destitute person, a down-and-out.
